questions.q: Why is a simulated Hadamard gate always mathematically exact, while a real hardware Hadamard gate is not?
options: Real hardware Hadamard gates always produce completely random results with no relation to the ideal gate
Simulators and real hardware are equally exact; there is no meaningful difference
Real hardware applies the Hadamard gate twice by mistake

A simulator performs an exact matrix multiplication with no physical process involved, while real hardware implements the gate as a physical pulse that can land slightly off from the ideal rotation (gate error)
questions.explain: A simulator computes the gate as pure arithmetic, which is exact by construction. Real hardware has to physically execute the gate via a pulse or similar control, which is subject to small imperfections — a gate error — that a simulator simply has no equivalent of.

questions.q: Why can a simulator report the exact probability of every circuit outcome, while real hardware can only estimate those probabilities?
options: Real hardware can inspect its own state vector just like a simulator, but chooses not to
Simulators and real hardware report probabilities in exactly the same way

A simulator has direct access to the underlying state-vector array at any point; real hardware collapses to one classical outcome per measurement, so probabilities must be estimated by running the whole circuit many times ('shots') and tallying results
Real hardware is simply programmed incorrectly by manufacturers
questions.explain: A simulator can print the full state vector because it is just an array in memory. A real measurement is a one-time physical collapse — there is no way to read probabilities directly, only to approximate them by repeating full runs ('shots') and counting outcomes.

questions.q: In the lesson's real 1,000-shot simulation of a Bell-state measurement (true probabilities exactly 0.5/0/0/0.5), the actual counts were 487/0/0/513 rather than 500/0/0/500. What does this demonstrate?
options: The simulation contains a bug because it didn't produce exactly 500/500

Finite sampling only approaches the true probabilities as shot count grows — it does not exactly match them for any finite number of shots, which is why real hardware results are reported as counts over N shots rather than exact probabilities
Sampling noise affects every outcome equally, including ones with exactly zero true probability
The Bell state's true probabilities are actually 0.487 and 0.513, not 0.5 and 0.5
questions.explain: 487/513 vs. the true 500/500 split is ordinary statistical sampling noise, not an error — it is exactly the gap between a simulator's exact probability and what any finite number of real shots on hardware would produce. The |01⟩/|10⟩ counts landed exactly at 0 because those true probabilities are exactly zero, so there was nothing to fluctuate around.

questions.q: Why does a simulator's applyCNOT(state, control, target, numQubits) function work identically for ANY pair of qubit indices, while real hardware cannot always apply CNOT directly between any two qubits?
options: Because real hardware has no concept of a 'control' or 'target' qubit
Because simulators cannot actually implement CNOT at all

Because real hardware has a fixed physical connectivity graph — two-qubit gates like CNOT generally only work directly between physically adjacent qubits, so non-adjacent qubits require extra SWAP gates to bring them together first
Because the applyCNOT function only works correctly for adjacent array indices as well
questions.explain: A simulator's array has no notion of physical adjacency, so any two indices can interact freely. Real qubits sit in a fixed physical layout, and two-qubit gates generally require physical adjacency — non-adjacent interactions need SWAP gates inserted first, costing extra depth and error exposure that a simulator never incurs.

questions.q: How does the lesson connect decoherence to Chapter 4's circuit-depth concept?
options: Every additional sequential gate layer (depth) is more elapsed real time, which is more opportunity for decoherence to degrade the qubit's state — making depth a correctness concern on real hardware, whereas on a simulator depth only affects runtime, never correctness
Decoherence only affects circuits with high width, not high depth
Decoherence makes deep circuits run faster on real hardware
Depth has no relationship to decoherence; they are unrelated hardware properties
questions.explain: Depth measures the longest sequential chain of gates a qubit must pass through. Since decoherence accumulates with elapsed time, a deeper circuit gives it more time to corrupt the state on real hardware — a cost that simply does not exist for a noiseless simulator.
